assumptions.subject: workload
assumptions.statement: 50,000 rps: 62% GET, 18% PUT, 15% HEAD/LIST, 3% DELETE. Read-dominated, which is what an object store is for. A further 2% is asynchronous reclaim work, modelled as its own flow because it is real load on the same components without sitting on any user's critical path.

assumptions.subject: metacache
assumptions.statement: 85% metadata cache hit on GET, 70% on HEAD/LIST. Metadata - not bytes - is the hot path of an object store: every request resolves a key to a placement before any data moves.

assumptions.subject: meta
assumptions.statement: The metadata index is SHARDED by bucket+key hash across 3 Postgres primaries. instances=3 here means three independent shards, not three copies of one database, so the engine's divide-arrivals-across-instances model is the correct shape for once.

assumptions.subject: data
assumptions.statement: Data nodes are modelled at ~6,000 object ops/s each. Real placement is erasure-coded (e.g. 8+3): one client PUT becomes 11 fragment writes across failure domains. The engine counts the client operation once, so internal write amplification on the data plane is NOT reflected here.

assumptions.subject: data
assumptions.statement: COST GAP, stated plainly: this design BUILDS an object store, so the data-plane nodes are your own hardware - and Keystone's grounded catalogue has no per-instance price for the `object_store` kind (AWS prices S3 per GB-month and per request, not per node). The data plane therefore reports $0, which is WRONG in the direction that flatters the design. The compute total below covers the front-end, metadata and background tiers only; disks, racks and replication bandwidth are unpriced.

assumptions.subject: durability
assumptions.statement: The product promise of an object store is DURABILITY (eleven nines), which comes from erasure coding across independent failure domains plus background scrub and repair. The v1 engine computes throughput, latency and cost - it has no durability model at all, so nothing below is evidence about data safety.

assumptions.subject: gc
assumptions.statement: A DELETE only writes a tombstone and emits an event - it does NOT wait for space to be reclaimed, which is why the GC workers sit on the `background_reclaim` flow and not on the synchronous delete path. Modelling them synchronously reported a ~180 ms DELETE, which was wrong about both the latency and the design. Workers run at ~1,500 ops/s each because each unit of work is heavyweight (read, verify, rewrite, delete); the continuous background scrub is additional load not represented here.

_library.summary: S3-style object store: stateless API front end over a sharded metadata index and an erasure-coded data plane.
